summary.text: A 79-year-old man with a history of hypertension on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor therapy and type II diabetes mellitus (ASA 2) was scheduled for transurethral resection of bladder. Preoperative assessment did not reveal a personal or family history of angioedema, and there were no previous anesthetic complications. Because of technical difficulties for spinal anesthesia, general anesthesia was used with a size 4 I-gel laryngeal mask airway, and the procedure lasted about 60 minutes.

Fifteen minutes after transfer to the post-anesthesia care unit he developed perioral edema of both upper and lower lips. An allergic reaction was initially suspected and chlorphenamine and dexamethasone were given, with no respiratory compromise, stridor or hemodynamic instability. He then revealed a history of hereditary angioedema, was transferred to the intensive care unit for close observation and received subcutaneous icatibant 30 mg.

The perioral swelling regressed within two hours without airway intervention. C1-Inhibitor levels measured in the subsequent days were below the normal range. He moved to the hospital ward the following day and was discharged without further complications. No prophylaxis had been given because hereditary angioedema was unknown, and airway manipulation with the laryngeal mask airway likely acted as a trigger.
